title: Batching Hysteresis & Cold-start Tail Investigation
body:
Summary:

Short: We ran a focused set of experiments to understand an uncomfortable correlation we saw in production p99 spikes: small, recurring cold-starts of worker processes + batch-formation hysteresis produce long tail latency events even when mean throughput is fine. This doc captures the experiment matrix, traces, lightweight profiles, hypotheses, and suggested mitigations.

Why this matters:
- Customer-facing SLOs are at 99th percentile, and although average latency is within SLO, p99 occasionally exceeds target by 2x–5x during low/variable QPS windows (especially tenant burst periods).
- These spikes are expensive to chase with more GPUs — root cause appears to be scheduling/formation behavior interacting with process-level cold starts and memory reclaim spikes.

Experiment goals:
1) Quantify contribution of worker cold-start (process init, JIT warmups, kernel selection) to tail.
2) Measure how hysteresis in batch-formation (time-based hold vs size-driven) amplifies cold-starts into long tails.
3) Validate mitigations: ephemeral warm pools, lower hysteresis thresholds, and light-weight prefetch/warm RPCs.

Test harness and environments:
- Replay traces from trace-id: replay/2024-10-31/tenant-42-lowburst (synthetic replayer running on perf cluster).
- Hardware: g5x2-like nodes (NVIDIA A-series equiv), 2x 80GB GPU per node, same as prod config.
- Runtime: runner v1.11.3 (with experimental kernel-selection logging).
- Prometheus + Jaeger + perf + small eBPF probes for syscalls.
- Trace windows: 30m per run, 10x repeats each config.

Key knobs under test:
- batch.max_size: 8, 16, 32
- batch.max_wait_ms (timeout): 1, 4, 10, 20
- batch.hysteresis_ms (extra wait when previous batch was below threshold): 0, 5, 15
- worker.warm_pool_size: 0, 1, 3 (number of idle warmed processes kept ready)
- worker.prefetch_rpc: off/on (RPC to pre-initialize model in process before first real request)

Experiment matrix (subset shown):
- A: baseline (max_size=32, max_wait=10, hysteresis=15, warm_pool=0)
- B: reduce hysteresis (hysteresis=0) keep others same
- C: small batches (max_size=8, max_wait=4, hysteresis=5)
- D: warm pool=1, hysteresis=15
- E: prefetch_rpc=on, warm_pool=0
- F: combined mitigation (warm_pool=1, hysteresis=0, max_wait=4)

Measurements collected:
- p50/p95/p99 latency for generation call (end-to-end).
- scheduler queue time distribution (time request spends waiting to be batched).
- worker init time (first request to process after spawn): process fork+import time, model load time, first-kernel-compile time if any.
- memory reclaim/GC events and page-fault rates from eBPF.
- timeline flamegraphs sampled at 50Hz during spikes.

Representative results (median over repeats):
- A (baseline): p50=18ms, p95=72ms, p99=420ms (large tail events 400–900ms seen in traces).
- B (no hysteresis): p50=20ms, p95=66ms, p99=160ms (significant reduction in tail).
- C (small batches): p50=24ms, p95=86ms, p99=220ms (worse p95, slightly better p99 versus baseline).
- D (warm pool=1): p50=19ms, p95=68ms, p99=140ms (warm pool reduces first-request penalty).
- E (prefetch_rpc): p50=19ms, p95=70ms, p99=150ms (similar to warm pool but less resource-heavy).
- F (combined): p50=21ms, p95=62ms, p99=120ms (best overall tail improvement).

Observations and profiling notes:
1) Cold-start cost breakdown (observed in worker init logs):
   - process fork + python import: 12–45ms, varies with memory pressure
   - model mmap + mmap faulting (first read): 35–120ms when page cache cold; eBPF shows hundreds of zero->soft page faults during this period
   - first-kernel-compiled op (when kernel not previously selected): 20–80ms intermittently
   Net: worker init median ~75ms, tail ~350ms when combined with heavy page faults.

2) Hysteresis amplification pattern:
   - When a previous batch was undersized (example: 3/32), we apply hysteresis_ms (15ms) to let a following request join the undersized batch. If no requests arrive, scheduler delays creating a batch by hysteresis_ms repeatedly (back-to-back), producing a queueing pattern that interacts with cold-starts:
     * Cold-starting a worker can take 100–400ms. Hysteresis keeps the scheduler waiting for small joiners instead of dispatching to a warmed worker or creating a new worker immediately. Result: requests wait longer than necessary on the queue, inflating p99.

3) Memory-pressure sensitivity:
   - Nodes with >75% committed memory (observed during other tenants' activity) had much higher mmap fault times. The same config produced 2–3x longer model load times and higher p99s.

4) Prefetch RPC vs Warm pool tradeoffs:
   - Warm pools keep processes pinned (uses more GPU memory and host memory depending on model residency). Warm pool=1 produced reliable reductions in p99 but increases idle memory footprint ~+350MB per pool entry for Llama2-13B config.
   - Prefetch RPC (send a lightweight dummy request to spin up process and touch pages) had similar tail reductions without persistent memory overhead but relies on timed scheduling and may increase network chatter.

5) Small batches (max_size=8) tended to increase overall token efficiency (more responsive per-request) but hurt p95 because batching opportunities are missed at slightly higher QPS due to smaller windows.

Concrete hypotheses (ranked):
- H1: Primary contributor to intermittent p99 spikes is worker cold-start/pagefault storm at first model access.
- H2: Secondary amplifier is scheduler hysteresis delaying dispatch for small-joiners; eliminating hysteresis reduces amplification even when cold-starts occur.
- H3: Under host memory pressure, cold-start penalty dominates and mitigation must focus on warmed memory or prefetching rather than scheduling adjustments alone.

Recommended mitigations to ship (short-term):
1) Set batch.hysteresis_ms = 0 by default for hosted tenants in low-QPS tiers (can be a feature flag). This gave the biggest single improvement without material cost.
2) Implement a lightweight prefetch_rpc hook in runner: when an idle worker pool is empty but node free capacity exists, send a periodic dummy request for tenants with bursty patterns. Controlled by tenant-level hints.
3) Add a node-local memory-pressure signal to scheduler: if host memory >70% used, prefer pre-warmed workers and avoid scheduling new spawns during bursts (or raise max_wait slightly to allow reuse).

Medium-term suggestions (Q1 roadmap):
- Warm-pool autoscaling with cost accounting in Console (customers can opt-in to keep N warmed processes). Offer a grace period pricing model.
- Page-prefetch during model deployment (touch mapped pages in advance) integrated into model lifecycle jobs so newly-deployed model versions pre-warm page cache on nodes likely to serve them.
- Kernel-compilation caching across processes (share compiled kernels in a sidecar).

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How often do page-fault storms occur across customers? (Need cross-tenant telemetry).
- Are there model architectures where kernel compilation happens on first forward significantly more often? Need to tag by model family.
- Explore whether ephemeral tiny workers (short-lived lightweight process that can forward to GPU resident process) can act as admission controllers to reduce cold-starts without full warm pools.

Quick runbook for on-call (if p99 spike observed):
1) Check "worker_init_time" histogram and "page_fault_rate" graph in tenant dashboard for recent spike window.
2) If page-fault-rate high -> scale up warm_pool for tenant or flag nodes with high memory pressure.
3) If hysteresis-driven queue waits (queue_time histogram shows many small waits ~hysteresis_ms) -> toggle hysteresis feature flag to 0 for tenant and monitor.
4) If repeated cold-starts cluster on nodes -> mark nodes for deeper memory reclamation investigation and coordinate with infra.

Notes and snippets (useful commands):
- Trace replay invocation used:
  ./tools/replay_trace --trace replay/2024-10-31/tenant-42-lowburst --duration 30m --concurrency 400 --target-runner runner-perf-01:8080

- Example Prometheus queries used during analysis:
  1) p99 generation latency: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(runner_request_duration_bucket[5m])) by (le))
  2) worker init time: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(runner_worker_init_seconds_bucket[10m])) by (le))
  3) node pagefault rate: rate(node_soft_page_faults_total[1m])

- Minimal eBPF script used to capture mmap faults (spawned for 5m windows) is checked into PR 482.

Appendix: raw excerpt from a spike trace (timestamps relative to trace start):
[00:03:12.102] incoming req id=501 queued
[00:03:12.117] scheduler waited for join (hysteresis 15ms)
[00:03:12.132] decision fork new worker -> worker pid=34221
[00:03:12.144] worker pid=34221 fork+import start
[00:03:12.360] worker pid=34221 mmap page faults (n=134)
[00:03:12.612] worker pid=34221 first-kernel-compile start
[00:03:13.020] worker ready, request dispatched -> end-to-end latency 918ms (p99 event)

Good next steps I will take:
- Add tenant-level feature flag for hysteresis override and run A/B on small subset of hosted tenants for 2 weeks.
- Wire up warm_pool usage telemetry to billing so product can evaluate pricing model.
- Broaden trace sampling to capture more page-fault stats across nodes and models.

Notes to self / rough TODOs:
- Draft a short note for product about warm pool pricing tradeoffs (Leah to review).
- Follow up with infra on kernel cache sidecar feasibility (Samir).
- Add an ops-automation script to flip hysteresis flag in emergency (on-call runbook).
